rationale.conceptual: The work uses established density functional theory and Boltzmann transport theory, both implemented in standard codes. While the technique is not novel, reproducing it demands careful construction of hybrid supercells (44–104 atoms), appropriate choice of k‑meshes, cutoffs, and convergence criteria, and linking DFT output to BoltzTraP – a non‑trivial multi‑part procedure typical of computational materials research.
rationale.execution: The pipeline spans geometry relaxation, self‑consistent and non‑self‑consistent electronic structure calculations, BoltzTraP transport runs, and post‑processing to extract maximum ZT_elec. It involves multiple interdependent stages with file handoffs for several systems and many temperatures. The tooling is standard (Quantum ESPRESSO, BoltzTraP), but orchestrating the sequential workflow and managing convergence across large supercells raises it above a simple two‑step script.

difficulty.reasoning: Applying standard DFT (Quantum ESPRESSO with PBE+vdW) and semiclassical Boltzmann transport (BoltzTraP, constant relaxation time) to compute thermoelectric performance of large hybrid supercells. The method is well-established but requires careful setup of supercells, convergence parameters, and linking DFT to transport post‑processing.

compute_estimate.reasoning: Plane‑wave DFT on supercells with up to 104 atoms and dense transport k‑meshes (up to 1600 k‑points) will dominate memory usage, requiring roughly 64 GB RAM; the paper acknowledges use of HPC CPU clusters, and no GPU acceleration is required.
